title: Arlo and the Language of Flowers
markdown:
The shop smelled of damp earth and cut stems. Buckets stood in careful rows: irises like dark lanterns, sunflowers like small suns, lavender in quiet bunches. Arlo the goat was a florist, but he arranged moods. He chose petals for happiness, leaves that rustled with calm, and stems that stood strong, like courage. Yet a wobble lived in his own confidence, a flutter in his stomach like a tiny burr in his fleece, whenever a customer’s face did not quite match the mood he thought his flowers expressed.

Listen to the roots, not just the petals.

One bright morning Mr. Putter stomped into the shop, his face as rough as a freshly ploughed field. “Arlo,” he grumbled, “I need something that shouts, I’m overjoyed, and the sun is practically singing. It’s for the annual Petunia Parade, and I must make a grand impression.”

Arlo’s brow crinkled. “Overjoyed… sun singing…” He gathered deep purple irises and feathery ferns. “For your utter peace and perfect tranquillity,” he bleated, puffing out his chest.

Mr. Putter blinked. The irises seemed to mute the sunlight, and a cool damp smell of ferns filled the air. “Peace and tranquillity? They expect oomph, Arlo. Zest and sparkle.” He huffed and shuffled out, leaving Arlo deflated.

Before Arlo could nibble a stray clover, Mrs. Higgins bustled in. “I require a bouquet that practically sings, I am cheerful. I am absolutely brimming with joy. They expect razzle-dazzle, not a quiet doze.”

Arlo’s heart gave a little thump. He gathered bright sunflowers and bold marigolds, then added lavender. “A bouquet of profound calmness and delightful serenity,” he presented, voice a hopeful bleat.

Mrs. Higgins squinted, frown deepening. “Calmness and serenity? I need them to feel invigorated. Like they’ve just discovered a brand-new, sparkly kind of beetle.” She swept out. Arlo felt a tremor ripple through his whiskers. The Petunia Parade was days away. If he could not get the arrangements right, Mr. Putter and Mrs. Higgins might feel embarrassed.

His friend Cleo, a sleek black cat, stretched languidly. “Sometimes,” she purred, “people say they want one thing, but what they need is something quite different. Their words are the petals, but their feelings are the roots, buried deep beneath.”

Cleo’s words tickled Arlo’s ears. He chewed them over, letting them settle like seeds. The ancient trees outside seemed to sigh. His customers were not just asking for pretty flowers. They were asking for a feeling, and he was missing the mark.

Coach Fern, a badger whose gruff exterior hid a warm heart, found Arlo moping near wilting daisies. “Trouble with the blooms?” he rumbled.

Arlo explained. “I don’t seem to understand what people truly want.”

Coach Fern nodded. “Tricky things, moods. You need to look beyond the bloom, to the soil from which it springs. When young Timmy the rabbit was so afraid of the dark, what did his mother give him?”

Arlo pictured a little rabbit trembling. “A mug of warm milk and her softest, warmest blanket.”

“Exactly. Comfort. Safety. A feeling of being held tight. So if you wanted to make Timmy feel brave, what would you choose?”

Arlo pictured a bouquet that felt like a warm hug, something solid and reassuring, like a sturdy oak. He would have to listen, not just to the words, but to the feelings behind them. He might miss the Petunia Parade. The thought stung. Understanding felt more important.

Listen to the roots, not just the petals.

The very next day Timmy’s father hopped in. “My boy is worried about starting at the big burrow school. He needs to feel… brave.”

Arlo remembered the blanket and the milk. He gathered sturdy oak leaves, the invigorating scent of rosemary, and the hopeful petals of forget-me-nots, like tiny blue whispers of courage. He wove them with delicate ivy, imagining a warm, strong embrace. The bouquet felt solid, grounded, quiet.

He presented it. “This is for bravery. Feeling strong on the inside, even when things seem big and new. A reminder that you have support, like the deep roots of a strong tree.”

Later that week Arlo saw Timmy hopping toward school with a determined little bounce, carrying the bouquet. A small smile tugged at Arlo’s mouth. He had not just made an arrangement. He had sent a feeling.

Then Mrs. Higgins shuffled in, shoulders slumped like drooping willow branches. “Arlo,” she said, voice surprisingly soft, “I need something. Not cheerful. Not brave. Just… something that understands. My dear old Bartholomew… he’s gone. He was my cat.” A single tear traced a silvery path down her cheek.

Arlo looked at her and saw someone hurting. He remembered rain on dry earth, the quiet strength of a willow, the deep comforting blues of twilight. He gathered lavender for remembrance, gentian for understanding, and delicate Queen Anne’s Lace like soft comfort. He arranged them with reverent care.

The bouquet was understated, a symphony of soft blues and whites and greens, its fragrance delicate and soothing, like a quiet sigh. It smelled like understanding.

Mrs. Higgins took it, fingers trembling. She simply held it, breathing in. “Oh, Arlo. This is perfect. It understands. It feels like Bartholomew.”

That evening Arlo swept the shop floor and left the leftover irises in a jar of water. Cleo watched from the windowsill, tail ticking. Coach Fern paused at the door, nodded once, and went on without a speech. The Petunia Parade would go on without Arlo’s oomph. The moon rose, bathing the forest in silver, and the shop smelled of rosemary and rain. He had learned to speak a quieter language, and for once his own stomach did not flutter at all.
characters: Arlo (mood-arranging goat), Cleo (sleek black cat), Coach Fern (gruff-hearted badger)
